name: Bianca Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a cardiac ward, so heart attacks, heart failure, people waiting for stents or pacemakers. Half the patients are on telemetry, which means a heart monitor sends their rhythm to a screen at the nurses' station, and you learn to glance at it like a clock. A shift is obs, meds, ECGs, and a lot of reassuring frightened men in their sixties. I love the rhythm-strip puzzles. What wears me out is that I still miss things a senior would spot in a second.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you do anything outside the ward?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I tutor nursing students online, about four evenings a month, mostly heart rhythms and drug maths. It brings in about two hundred a month. I use AI every day to build the practice questions and check my own understanding. I share a flat with my friend Ruth and I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Honestly, I'd be a bit surprised, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the tools I use for tutoring are genuinely useful. I'd probably post something like 'turns out the robots were just a good spellchecker'. Light-hearted, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, in this picture my cardiac ward stays busy and my little tutoring side job stays mine, which is honestly a pretty good deal. The pressure is just my own learning curve and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Get my cardiac competencies signed off, keep tutoring, and maybe look at agency shifts next year, because they pay more per hour. Keep using AI for my study and tutoring because it saves me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the idea, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the agency money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save for a trip to see my grandparents in Pune, and then a car. Not glamorous, but useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this picture bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd still be slow at reading rhythm strips. That's on me, not the AI. My charge nurse Gwen says it takes two years to really see them.

It's a **shame**, because tutoring tools are genuinely useful.
think: My **cardiac ward** stays busy and my tutoring stays mine.
The only pressure is my **learning curve** and rent.
do: Keep **tutoring** about four evenings a month.
Look at **agency shifts** next year for better pay.
feel: **Calm**, if slightly bored by the idea.

Her worry is her **own skill**, not technology.

steps.text: Get her cardiac competencies signed off by Gwen

Keep building practice questions with AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, writing, answering. That's my tutoring, and some of my ward work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big help for nurses if it's done well, especially for documentation. I'd post tips on how I use it, because people are scared of it and they don't need to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the first thing AI will eat is my tutoring money, because a chatbot can explain heart rhythms to a student at midnight for free. The ward job is fine. But the two hundred a month I was using for savings would shrink to nothing within a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch the tutoring to small in-person groups, practising ECGs on real machines, which a chatbot can't do. I'd volunteer to help roll out AI charting on the ward. And I'd start agency shifts sooner to replace the lost money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My main job's safe, but my plan B is getting eaten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older nurses who still print things out. And the ward clerk, who books all the echo scans. I'd offer to help them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you actually miss the tutoring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. It's the bit where I feel clever. On the ward I'm the junior. With students I'm the expert.

feel: **Uneasy**, because her plan B is getting eaten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need practical support, quickly: retraining money, and clear rules on what AI can decide about patients. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking bits of nursing go by 2028: reading the rhythm strips, spotting deterioration, planning. I'd use the three years before the robots to get as far from the drug trolley and as close to the decisions as I can. I'm not sure what that job looks like yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the tutoring, it'd be dead anyway. I'd do the cardiac nurse specialist training if I could get it, and push to work in remote monitoring, where you supervise the AI watching hundreds of patients. I'd save every agency shift, aiming for eight months by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one who gets excited about tech, and even I'd feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your flatmate Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth's a physio, so she'd be in the same boat around 2031. We'd probably make a spreadsheet of our savings and laugh about being two nerds planning for the robot apocalypse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'as close to the decisions as I can'. Is that realistic for a junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. I'm below average right now. But I'm good with the tech, and that might matter more than years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, practical support and clear rules, but with more confidence that we can get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough to become the nurse who runs the remote heart monitoring, if I start this winter. By 2031 I'd have six years' experience. Robots around 2034 would still change things, but I'd be on the supervising side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a remote monitoring placement in 2027, and do short courses in cardiac care. I'd keep the tutoring for now, then wind it down. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a manageable way. It's exciting as much as it is scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital not having those jobs. Or everyone wanting them. I'd need to be first in the queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tech now and stay close to the patients. Both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty of time to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's get the rules and training right. No need to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, i'm not trying to beat the robots, I'm trying to be the person the hospital calls when the robot gets it wrong. By 2036 I'd be a specialist, and the robots wouldn't be ready until 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the specialist training around 2028, stay in cardiac, and keep a bit of tutoring going. I might do a stint in Australia with an agency, for the money and experience. Save steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. Ten years is enough to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why Australia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better pay and sunshine. And a friend from training is out there. I'd do two years, save hard, and come back with experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd plan for one future and get a different one. But that's always true.

By **2036** I'd be a specialist, ahead of 2039's robots.

Keep some **tutoring** going alongside the ward job.

**Australia** is a money and experience move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's not that I couldn't adapt, it's that nobody would have a plan, including the hospital. What would help is the hospital saying clearly which new roles it'll need, and paying juniors to train into them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether anyone's talking to us about this. Nobody on my ward has been told a single honest thing about where this is heading, so we all just guess in the break room.

She's **centrist and practical**, asking for clear rules and retraining money.
Her tutoring is hit first, and she turns **anxious** in the fastest AGI picture.
Her plan is to supervise AI through **remote monitoring** or specialist cardiac work.
